standard.title: Algorithms with branching and iteration
standard.description: follow and describe algorithms involving sequencing, comparison operators (branching) and iteration
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can follow and describe algorithms involving a sequence of steps, branching and iteration (AC9TDI2P02). They have encountered these three structures but at a descriptive, recognition level. They have not yet worked with comparison operators explicitly or described algorithms involving numerical conditions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students follow and describe algorithms that use sequencing, comparison operators (e.g. greater than, equal to) as branching conditions, and iteration (repeating steps a fixed number of times or until a condition is met).

nodes.label: Sequencing as ordered steps
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can follow a multi-step algorithm and identify where they are in the sequence
nodes.minimum_width: Follow a written or diagrammatic algorithm with at least four steps; identify the current step when paused mid-sequence
nodes.typical_width: Follow algorithms in different representations (list of steps, simple diagram, recipe format); track progress through the sequence; identify if a step has been skipped and what effect that has
wider: Follow algorithms that describe First Nations Australian practices with strict ordering requirements (e.g. step sequences for preparing traditional foods or caring for specific animals) — discuss why step order matters in these contexts
Compare two algorithms for the same task with different step orders — identify which is more efficient or which produces better results and explain why
success_criteria: Follows a multi-step algorithm without skipping steps
Can identify which step they are at when asked mid-sequence
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot track their position in a sequence cannot attempt N2 or N3 — branching and iteration both require knowing where you are in the algorithm before deciding or repeating.

nodes.label: Comparison operators as branching conditions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe a branch in an algorithm using a comparison operator (e.g. if UV index > 3, if score = 10) and explain what each path does
nodes.minimum_width: Given an algorithm with one branch using a comparison (e.g. if temperature is above 25°C), trace both paths and describe what happens in each case
nodes.typical_width: Describe algorithms with multiple branches using comparison operators (greater than, less than, equal to) involving numbers and text; trace the correct path for different input values
wider: Describe algorithms that branch on comparisons involving culturally specific conditions — for example, IF a certain animal is found in a ranger survey THEN a specific protocol applies; discuss how the comparison drives the decision
Explore algorithms involving combined conditions (e.g. IF UV index > 3 AND it is a school day) — describe what the combined comparison checks for

response_modes.reason: Comparison operators abstract quickly from the concrete case. Students who only see one type of comparison (e.g. 'greater than' with temperature) may not recognise that text comparisons, equal-to checks, and multi-condition branches follow the same logic. Multiple contexts build the generalised pattern.

Tracing both branches of a conditional requires holding two cases simultaneously. Students benefit from explicit scaffolding: 'what happens if the condition is true? what happens if it is false?' before attempting to write their own branches.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The comparison operator node is a genuine hinge point — students who cannot connect comparison conditions to branching behaviour will struggle to implement programs in AC9TDI4P04. The wider tier (combined conditions, real-world protocol branches) adds meaningful context without exceeding the band.
success_criteria: Correctly traces both branches of an algorithm with a comparison condition
Names the comparison operator (greater than, equal to, etc.) used in the branch
nodes.hinge_reason: Comparison operators are directly prerequisite for implementing branching in AC9TDI4P04 — students who cannot identify the condition and trace both paths cannot write a working conditional program.

nodes.label: Iteration as repeating steps
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe an algorithm that repeats steps a fixed number of times and explain what changes with each repetition
nodes.minimum_width: Follow an algorithm that repeats a step a set number of times (e.g. add a number 5 times to compute a product); describe what the algorithm does and what changes in each repetition
nodes.typical_width: Describe algorithms with iteration for different purposes — fixed-count repetition (multiply using repeated addition), and repetition until a condition is met; identify what is constant and what changes across iterations
wider: Describe iteration in algorithms used for monitoring tasks — for example, an algorithm that counts sightings of a specific animal in a survey by repeating a tally step; discuss how the repetition connects to the data being collected
Explore an algorithm that combines iteration and branching — describe how repetition and decisions interact (e.g. 'check each item on a list; IF it matches THEN record it')

response_modes.reason: Students often understand iteration from one context (e.g. counting) but do not recognise it in others (processing a list, animating movement, repeating a procedure). Multiple contexts build a functional understanding of 'do this repeatedly' across varied algorithmic uses.

success_criteria: Identifies that steps are repeated in an iterative algorithm
States what changes between repetitions (e.g. a count increases, a position moves)

nodes.label: Describing complete algorithms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe an algorithm that combines sequencing, branching and iteration in their own words or using a diagram
nodes.minimum_width: Given an algorithm with all three structures, describe what it does in plain language — identifying where the sequence is, where a decision occurs, and where repetition happens
nodes.typical_width: Describe algorithms of different complexity using written descriptions and diagrams; explain the purpose of the algorithm and how each structure contributes to achieving it
wider: Describe an algorithm for a First Nations ranger protocol that involves all three structures — for example, a monitoring procedure with a fixed number of survey loops, conditional recording rules, and sequential reporting steps
Describe and compare two algorithms that solve the same problem differently (e.g. two routes to the same location with different decision points) — explain why both are valid and how they differ

response_modes.reason: Describing a combined algorithm requires recognising that sequencing, branching and iteration are not separate things but work together in a single logical structure. The integration challenge is seeing how the structures interlock — this node is where that coordination is the learning.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one example each of sequencing, branching and iteration in a described algorithm
Description matches what the algorithm actually does
